youtube.pinnedComment: The rule that saves you grief: your RAM and your motherboard must be the SAME DDR generation. The notch moves every time on purpose — it's a physical lock so you can't fry a stick at the wrong voltage. 👇 What's in your machine? Subscribe — 'How a CPU Works' is next.
youtube.hook: That stick of RAM is more interesting than it looks: the notch is in a very particular place, the pins a very particular number — get the wrong one and it won't even fit the slot. Let's decode every type of memory, from DDR1 to DDR5 and the whole family beyond the desktop.

segments.narration: That stick of R-A-M in your computer is far more interesting than it looks. The notch is in one very particular place, the pins are a very particular number, and get the wrong one — it won't even physically fit the slot. So let's decode every type of memory: the five generations of D-D-R, from two thousand to today — each one faster, cooler, and deliberately incompatible with the last — and then the whole family beyond the desktop: the laptop stick, the soldered phone memory, the graphics-card speed demon, and the blazing cache hiding inside your C-P-U.

segments.name: DDR1
segments.narration: We start the ladder in the year two thousand, with the original D-D-R — now called D-D-R-1. 'D-D-R' stands for double data rate: it moves data on both the up and the down of each clock tick, doubling the throughput of the older S-D-R-A-M. A desktop stick has one hundred eighty-four pins, runs at two-point-five volts, and tops out around three gigabytes a second. Modest by today's standards — but it set the template that every single generation since has followed.
segments.verdict: The original double-data-rate stick — the template for everything after.

segments.name: DDR2
segments.narration: Three years later came D-D-R-2. The pin count jumps to two hundred and forty, the voltage drops to one-point-eight, and clever buffering roughly doubles the bandwidth again, to around eight gigabytes a second. And here's the crucial detail you can actually see with your eyes: the notch — that little gap in the gold pins — sits in a different spot than on D-D-R-1. That is completely deliberate. It's a physical key, so you literally cannot push a D-D-R-2 stick into a D-D-R-1 slot.
segments.verdict: More pins, less voltage, a moved notch — and twice the speed.

segments.name: DDR3
segments.narration: D-D-R-3 arrived in two thousand and seven, and had an astonishingly long life — it powered P-Cs for the better part of a decade. It keeps two hundred and forty pins, but drops to one-point-five volts and pushes bandwidth up to around seventeen gigabytes a second. Now, note the trap: D-D-R-2 and D-D-R-3 both have two hundred and forty pins, so they look almost identical — but the notch is in a different place, so they still will not fit each other's slots. Always check the notch.
segments.verdict: A decade-long workhorse — same pin count as DDR2, but a different key.

segments.name: DDR4
segments.narration: D-D-R-4, from twenty fourteen, was the mainstream standard for years, and still fills millions of machines today. Pins climb to two hundred and eighty-eight, voltage falls again, to one-point-two, and bandwidth reaches the mid-twenties of gigabytes per second. D-D-R-4 also has a subtly curved bottom edge, slightly higher in the middle, which makes it easier to insert and seat evenly. Same shape family as before — but, you guessed it, a brand-new notch position all of its own.
segments.verdict: The long-running mainstream — 288 pins, a curved edge, lower power.

segments.name: DDR5
segments.narration: And the current flagship: D-D-R-5, from twenty twenty. It also carries two hundred and eighty-eight pins, but it's a big architectural leap. Each stick is split into two independent thirty-two-bit sub-channels for better efficiency, the voltage drops to just one-point-one, and the power-management chip that used to live on the motherboard now sits right on the stick itself. Bandwidth explodes past thirty-eight, and up beyond sixty gigabytes a second. And there's a new notch again, of course — so no, your D-D-R-4 will not fit.
segments.verdict: The current flagship — split channels, on-board power, and huge bandwidth.

segments.narration: Let's make that notch rule unmistakable, because it trips people up constantly. Every single D-D-R generation deliberately moves the notch to a new position. It is a physical lock. You cannot force a D-D-R-4 stick into a D-D-R-5 board, or a D-D-R-3 into a D-D-R-4 — the key simply will not line up, and that is entirely on purpose, to stop you frying a stick at the wrong voltage. So the first rule of buying R-A-M: your memory and your motherboard must be the same D-D-R generation. No adapters, no exceptions.

segments.name: SO-DIMM
segments.narration: Same D-D-R chips, different shape. A So-D-I-M-M — a small-outline D-I-M-M — is the stubby stick made for laptops and mini-P-Cs, where a full-length desktop module simply won't fit. It's roughly half the length, with its own pin count — a D-D-R-4 So-D-I-M-M has two hundred and sixty pins. It clips in flat, rather than standing upright. Same underlying technology and the same speeds as its desktop cousin — just neatly folded into a much smaller space.
segments.verdict: Desktop DDR, laptop-sized — clips in flat to save space.

segments.name: LPDDR
segments.narration: L-P-D-D-R — low-power D-D-R — is the memory in your phone, your tablet, and most thin-and-light laptops, including Apple's M-series. It's engineered obsessively for battery life, sipping far less power than desktop D-D-R. But here's the catch: to save space and power, it is soldered directly onto the mainboard — there is no slot, and no stick. That makes it faster to reach the chip, but completely non-upgradable. The R-A-M you buy on day one is the R-A-M you are keeping forever.
segments.verdict: Battery-first memory, soldered down — what you buy is what you keep.

segments.name: GDDR
segments.narration: G-D-D-R — graphics D-D-R — is a specialised cousin, built for one job: feeding a G-P-U. A graphics card has to shovel an enormous amount of data for every single frame, so G-D-D-R, like today's G-D-D-R-6, trades the low latency of regular R-A-M for raw, massive bandwidth — hundreds of gigabytes a second. The chips are soldered in a ring right around the G-P-U on the card, on a very wide bus. It's the same core D-D-R idea, but tuned entirely for throughput, over absolutely everything else.
segments.verdict: DDR tuned purely for bandwidth — soldered around the GPU.

segments.name: HBM
segments.narration: When even G-D-D-R isn't enough, there's H-B-M — high-bandwidth memory. Instead of spreading chips flat across a board, H-B-M stacks the memory dies vertically, in a tower, and places them right next to the processor on a shared silicon base called an interposer. Short connections, plus a gigantic bus, give it bandwidth measured in terabytes a second. It is expensive and complex, so you'll only find it where money is no object: the A-I accelerators, like Nvidia's H-100, that train the large models.
segments.verdict: Memory stacked in 3D for terabytes/sec — the RAM of AI chips.

segments.name: ECC Memory
segments.narration: E-C-C — error-correcting code — memory is about one single thing: never being wrong. Cosmic rays and electrical noise can occasionally flip a bit in R-A-M, which for your gaming P-C means a rare crash, but for a bank or a hospital server could mean quietly corrupted data. So E-C-C adds an extra memory chip that stores check-bits, letting it detect and silently fix single-bit errors on the fly. You pay a little more money, and a tiny bit of speed, in exchange for memory you can genuinely trust.
segments.verdict: An extra chip that catches bit-flips — memory you can trust.

segments.name: SRAM — the Cache
segments.narration: Finally, the fastest R-A-M of all — one you can't buy as a stick, because it lives inside your C-P-U. Everything so far has been D-R-A-M, built from leaky capacitors that need constant refreshing. S-R-A-M — static R-A-M — instead stores each bit in six transistors locked in a stable loop. No capacitor, no refresh, so it's dramatically faster — but each bit takes far more space, and far more money. That is why there's only a tiny amount of it, used as the C-P-U's L1, L2, and L3 cache: the small, blazing-fast scratchpad right beside the cores.
segments.verdict: The fastest RAM there is — tiny, pricey, hiding in your CPU as cache.

segments.question: What type of RAM is in your machine?
segments.narration: So that's memory, from the humble D-D-R-1 stick to the terabyte-a-second stacks inside an A-I supercomputer. The through-line: it is nearly all D-R-A-M — leaky capacitors in a grid — just packaged for a hundred different jobs, and the one rule that saves you real grief is to match the notch. We even ended up inside the processor, with S-R-A-M cache — which is the perfect place to go next: how a C-P-U actually works, four billion transistors in a single clock tick. If this demystified the stick, subscribe. So tell me — what type of R-A-M is living in your machine?
